column3: Near-verbatim parallel: a future assurance of patience is explicitly qualified by "if Allah wills."
The opening of Moses's journey supplies the immediate narrative setting for his later commitment.
Patient, righteous people receive forgiveness and a great reward, broadly affirming the promised patience.
Another future assurance using "if Allah wills," though it promises righteousness rather than patience and obedience.
Moses's request to follow a divinely taught guide directly precedes his pledge to endure that instruction.
Disobeying Allah and His messenger establishes the serious moral force of the focus's non-disobedience pledge.
The guide's repeated finding that Moses cannot remain patient directly tests the focus's promise.
This is travel context before the meeting, without clarifying patience, divine willing, or obedience.
It joins failure to follow with disobedience of an order, though in a different leadership dispute.
Job is praised as patient, providing a strong but general model of steadfast obedience.
The immediately following condition defines the required patience: do not question until the guide explains.
Adam's disobedience to his Lord gives a consequential contrast to the focus's pledge not to disobey.
It affirms dependence on Allah's will for revelation, but not a human future pledge or patience.
Journey fatigue is only distant preparation for the later test of patience.
Trials are paired with glad tidings for the patient, broadly supporting the focus's promised endurance.
The conditional phrase concerns Allah granting worldly goods, not a committed act of patience.
The guide first states that Moses will be unable to be patient, immediately provoking the focus's reply.
Allah's complete knowledge does not clarify the focus's patience, contingent commitment, or obedience.
The brief oath about angels administering a command has no material link to the focus.
The servant's forgotten fish and report remain part of the journey but do not illuminate the pledge.
The inability of false gods to create is unrelated to the focus's stated commitment.
Jacob's "beautiful patience" models steadfast trust under an unresolved trial.
The guide explains why Moses will lack patience when he does not encompass the relevant knowledge.
Pharaoh's denial and disobedience form a clear negative contrast to the focus's refusal to disobey.
Polytheists misuse "if Allah had willed" as an excuse, contrasting with the focus's humble contingency.
Moses turns back to seek the intended meeting place; it is only narrative preparation.
Disobedience and transgression explain a communal curse but offer only a general contrast.
It rejects fatalistic appeals to Allah's will and links them with following conjecture, contrasting the focus's sincere formula.
The separation and promised explanation conclude the patience failure anticipated in the focus.
The direct command to practice beautiful patience closely reinforces the focus's pledged patience.
Its divorce procedure and warning about legal limits do not clarify this instructional pledge.
The divinely taught servant is the guide whom Moses undertakes to follow patiently.
Divine sovereignty and witnesshood do not meaningfully develop the focus's themes.
Jacob answers a deceptive report with beautiful patience and appeal to Allah for help.
The final explanation explicitly returns to what Moses could not bear patiently.
Patience, truthfulness, devotion, and predawn seeking forgiveness form a compatible but general virtue cluster.
Believers may not retain a competing choice once Allah and His messenger decide an affair, strongly framing obedience.
Moses's first interruption shows the initial breach of the patience promised in the focus.
Its prohibition on unqualified claims about tomorrow is the immediate Quranic frame for the focus's "if Allah wills."
Marriage restrictions and Allah's watchfulness do not clarify the focus's commitment.
Moses asks pardon after forgetting, the first concrete failure of his pledge.
Patience and gratitude appear in a distinct historical lesson with little connection to the focal contract.
The messenger's response to disobedience distinguishes himself from wrongful deeds, a broad obedience contrast.
Moses accepts that another question ends their companionship, intensifying the contract he pledged to keep.
Fear of punishment for disobeying one's Lord reinforces the moral seriousness of refusing disobedience.
Mary's provision from Allah does not clarify the focus's patience or obedience.
Moses's objection to unpaid repair is the final act that breaks the patience condition.
It warns that the messenger cannot simply obey followers' preferences and praises aversion to disobedience.
Israel's refusal to remain patient and preference for the inferior give a narrative contrast to steadfast obedience.
We hear and disobey is an explicit opposite to the focus's pledge not to disobey an order.
Allah's power over revelation supports dependence on Him but not the focus's specific undertaking.
The garden's full yield does not bear on patience, divine willing, or obedience here.
The insufficiency of wealth and children for disbelievers is outside the focus's themes.
Choosing to remember gives only a distant link to the future-oriented expression of will.
Jesus's declaration of servanthood and prophethood does not clarify the focus's pledge.
Pharaoh's belated admission after a life of disobedience contrasts with a commitment meant to govern conduct beforehand.
Allah's conclusive proof and universal ability to guide provide only a broad divine-will context.
Allah's knowledge of all things does not illuminate the focus's patient obedience.
Noah conditions the arrival of punishment on Allah's will, a limited formula parallel without a pledge of action.
The question of human creation has no material relation to the focus.
Solomon's refusal of a gift concerns valuing divine provision, not this commitment.
The faithful are characterized by patience and reliance on their Lord, broadly supporting the focus's posture.
Satan's vow to obstruct the straight path does not clarify the focus.
Satan is characterized as disobedient to the Merciful, supplying a negative contrast to vowed obedience.
The speakers qualify their hoped-for guidance with "if Allah wills," but it lacks the focus's patience and order.
Human willing is explicitly dependent on Allah's willing, providing the theological basis for the focus's qualification.
The regretful claim that Allah did not guide me is only a remote divine-will parallel.
Fear of the great day for disobeying one's Lord supports the seriousness of obedient conduct.
Willing remembrance is a general response to admonition, not a close parallel to the focus.
Waiting patiently for the messenger to emerge provides a limited procedural parallel to patient restraint.
Wanting to be upright is a broad voluntary orientation without the focus's formula or obedience context.
The concise command to be patient for the Lord directly reinforces the central virtue pledged in the focus.
The messenger's lack of independent power apart from Allah's will is only a general theological parallel.
Creation in measured kinds does not clarify the focus's commitment.
Salih refuses a course that would mean disobeying Allah, giving a direct moral parallel.
John's freedom from disobedience is a broad character parallel without the focus's instructional setting.
Adam's provision in Paradise does not illuminate patience or obedience in the focus.
Patience and God-consciousness amid hostility support endurance, though the setting is military.
The oath concerning angels administering a command has no substantive relation to the focus.
Enduring the Fire after judgment contrasts with timely patience but is too remote for stronger relevance.
The dialogue about deifying Jesus and Mary does not clarify the focus's pledge.
Battlefield patience and God-consciousness provide only a context-specific endurance parallel.
Following revelation and lacking unseen knowledge weakly resonate with learning from guidance.
Human contentiousness and Quranic examples do not address the focus's patient obedience.
Abraham's confidence in Allah's all-encompassing knowledge is not a close neighbour of the focus.
Moses's offer of a manifest sign does not clarify the later pledge to Khidr.
A man's warning to Moses to flee is unrelated to the focus's themes.
Noah pairs disobeying him with following those whose wealth and children increase loss, highlighting the object of following.
Allah's creative command in Mary's annunciation does not clarify the focus.
Rules of kinship inheritance and group membership do not illuminate patient obedience.
The prophet's command to fear Allah and obey him gives a direct, though general, obedience parallel.
Allah's knowledge of what is hidden or disclosed does not clarify the focus's commitment.
Allah's self-sufficiency has no material connection to the focus.
Divine dominion and protection do not elucidate patience, willing, or obedience here.
Inheritance allocations do not clarify the focus's themes.
Taking a path to one's Lord by willing gives a meaningful but less exact counterpart to the focus's qualified resolve.
Creation, resurrection, and return to Allah do not clarify this promise.
Prayer, moral responsibility, and patience under what befalls form a disciplined obedience parallel.
Modesty regulations do not materially clarify the focus's promise.
Patient servants receive exalted reward, affirming the value of the patience Moses promises.
The indispensable continuation: future intentions must be qualified by "if Allah wills," exactly explaining the focus's formula.
Moses's first protest at the scuttled boat is the first narrated breach of his promise not to challenge the guide.
Moses's second protest at the killing is the repeated failure of the patience and non-interference pledged in the focus.
The explanation of the boat reveals the protective purpose that was hidden when Moses objected, vindicating deferred judgment.
The explanation of the boy's case discloses a concealed future harm, further explaining why patience was required.
The hoped-for replacement shows that the guide's troubling act was ordered toward mercy and a better outcome.
Jacob's future assurance, "you will enter Egypt, if Allah wills, secure," is a close formula parallel.
Allah's promise of future entry into the Sacred Mosque is expressly qualified by "if Allah wills," directly paralleling the focus's speech.
The garden owners swear to harvest in the morning, providing the setup for the warning about unqualified future resolve.
They make no exception to their plan, a pointed contrast to Moses's explicit "if Allah wills."
It joins obeying Allah and His messenger with patience and forbids conduct that weakens the community.
The command to follow revelation and be patient until Allah judges closely matches obedient, sustained restraint.
It combines patience for the Lord's judgment with refusing obedience to a sinner or denier.
Believers are warned of trials and told that patience and God-consciousness are matters of firm resolve.
The command to be patient, persevere, and remain vigilant gives a strong general ethic of sustained obedience.
The direct command to be patient and assurance that Allah does not lose the reward of good-doers supports the pledge.
Patient endurance seeking the Lord's face models the God-directed purpose of steadfastness.
The command to be patient, with patience possible only through Allah, complements the focus's dependence on divine willing.
It joins patience with regular praise of Allah, framing endurance as sustained devotional discipline.
Maintaining prayer and being patient in it gives a concrete form of obedient perseverance.
Patient certainty in Allah's signs is the condition associated with divinely guided leadership.
The patient are promised an immeasurable reward, affirming the value of the disposition Moses promises.
Patience and forgiveness are named as matters requiring firm resolve, matching the focus's forward commitment.
The messenger is commanded to be patient as resolute messengers were patient, a direct prophetic endurance parallel.
The command to be patient for the Lord's judgment, coupled with Jonah's impatient episode, closely cautions against Moses's later failures.
Patience over hostile speech and dignified withdrawal provide a general discipline of restraint.
Remembering the Lord morning and evening gives a devotional practice that sustains the focus's God-dependent resolve.
Faith, righteous action, truth, and mutual exhortation to patience place patience within ongoing communal obedience.
Believers are commanded to seek help through patience and prayer, giving a foundational practice of God-dependent endurance.
The believers' plea for patience and firmness under trial supplies a communal model of endurance.
The command to obey Allah, the messenger, and entrusted authority provides a general frame for the focus's pledge of obedience.
Moses tells his people to seek Allah's help and be patient, a particularly close Moses-centered parallel of dependent endurance.
The command to be patient until Allah judges gives a direct pattern of restraint while an outcome remains concealed.
God-consciousness and patience are joined with Allah's preservation of the reward of those who do good.
The command for gracious patience offers a direct but general model of restrained response.
Persevering patience in worship gives a devotional form of the steadfastness Moses promises.
Ishmael, Idris, and Dhu al-Kifl are named among the patient, providing prophetic exemplars of endurance.
Believers are described as patient under what befalls them and responsive to Allah's mention.
Allah identifies the patient as the successful recipients of reward, affirming the value of the pledged trait.
Life's social trials are explicitly posed as a test of whether people will be patient.
Those who patiently repel evil with good receive a doubled reward, showing active moral endurance.
Those who are patient and rely on their Lord are promised a dwelling in Paradise.
The command to be patient and not be unsettled by those lacking certainty closely fits steadfast resolve.
Frequent remembrance of Allah and patience are paired among the defining qualities of faithful men and women.
The prophet is commanded to be patient over opposition, with David recalled as a devoted servant.
Patience is commanded because Allah's promise is true, alongside seeking forgiveness and praise.
Responding to evil with what is better is attainable only through patience, portraying patience as active discipline.
Allah declares that He will test believers in order to make known those who strive and are patient.
The command to be patient for the Lord's judgment is joined to ongoing praise under divine watch.
The warning not to let wealth and children distract from Allah's remembrance supplies a practical threat to sustained God-directed resolve.
Paradise and silk are promised in return for patience, affirming its enduring outcome.
